latest.title: How the US solar industry remains resilient through sharp swings in energy policy
latest.notes: Conditions have been challenging for the US solar industry over the past couple of years, as Washington’s energy priorities have shifted dramatically. Yet the industry has remained resilient, thanks in part to rapid growth in demand for electricity to power data centres. The key question for solar suppliers now is not how far they can cut greenhouse gas emissions, but how fast they can bring new generation capacity on line. In this special episode from the RE+ conference in Las Vegas, Ed Crooks is joined by two leaders in US solar to discuss their perspectives on the changing outlook for the industry. Karen Bazela is the senior vice president of sales at Shoals Technologies Group, and Jessica Lawrence-Vaca is the chief commercial officer at Array Technologies. The two companies have announced a merger, with the aim of creating an integrated supplier for the solar and storage industries, including electrical balance of system solutions and trackers. Karen and Jessica discuss speed to power as a central advantage of solar. With long lead times for other generation technologies such as gas turbines, solar can help meet near-term demand while other sources come online. Policy whiplash has created challenges for the solar industry, but Karen and Jessica argue that it should be possible to get past some of the partisan division that has characterized the political debate over energy in recent years. They argue that policymakers should take an all-of-the-above approach, and reform permitting to expedite investment. Jessica says the solar industry also needs to do a better job of advocating for itself. She argue that it needs to make a stronger case around American manufacturing, construction jobs, steel and energy security, not only climate benefits. The domestic supply chain offers shorter lead times and more responsive service, but it comes with trade-offs. Karen says Shoals manufactures in the US while still sourcing some components overseas. Jessica says Array makes 85 to 90 per cent of its components in the US and recently opened a $50 million Albuquerque facility. The guests say a fully domestic supply chain cannot be built overnight, and that policy needs to distinguish between components that make sense to produce in America and those that do not. They note that trackers qualify for the 45X manufacturing tax credit, while electrical balance-of-systems equipment does not. Finally, Karen and Jessica discuss their positions as high-profile women in leadership roles in an industry that remains male-dominated. They argue that there is a need to recruit more women and show that they can have pathways into senior roles, and they talk about the work they are doing to highlight the opportunities that the industry has to offer. For more on careers for women in renewable energy, resources are available from Women in Renewable Energy ( https://womeninrenewableenergy.ca/ ) and Women of Renewable Industries and Sustainable Energy ( https://wrisenergy.org/ ). This episode of the Energy Gang is brought to you by Shoals Technologies, a leading provider of electrical balance of systems (EBOS) solutions for solar, energy storage, and data centers. As electricity demand surges, the race is on to deliver solar projects faster, smarter, and more reliably. In this episode, leaders from Shoals Technologies and Array Technologies explore how smarter power distribution, solar trackers, domestic manufacturing, and streamlined installation can reduce complexity, accelerate construction, and bring reliable power online faster. latest.title: Ethan Zindler and Lily Bermel on Clean Energy's Headwinds and Tailwinds
latest.notes: Earlier this month, US voters handed Democrats control of both chambers of Congress and flipped several governorships across the country. The dramatic shift in power raises big questions about where US energy policy is headed. Following the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act—which ended or cut back many of the Inflation Reduction Act's clean energy tax credits—analysts warned that new clean power additions could fall by more than half over the next decade. But the buildout has held up better than many expected. Last year, the US added more new power capacity than it had in over two decades, most of it coming from clean energy sources. Rising electricity demand, much of it from data centers, keeps pushing developers to build. Recent analyses suggest the clean energy buildout will keep growing, even without the full set of tax incentives. So what does the incoming Congress mean for clean energy policy? Should Democrats spend their political capital on restoring the tax credits or on clearing bottlenecks like permitting? With hyperscalers heavily relying on new natural gas capacity, how can policymakers make the case for clean energy heading into 2028? Today on the show, Jason Bordoff talks to Ethan Zindler and Lily Bermel about how Trump administration policies have impacted the state of clean energy in the US. Ethan Zindler is a non-resident fellow at the Center on Global Energy Policy (CGEP) and leads country and policy research at BloombergNEF (BNEF). Lily Bermel is a visiting fellow at CGEP and also consults with climate philanthropies on clean industrial strategy. Credits: Hosted by Jason Bordoff, Bill Loveless, and Daniel Sternoff. Produced by Mary Catherine O'Connor, Dara Diamond, and Kyu Lee. Engineering by Gregory Vilfranc.

latest.title: [Episode #287] – Clearing the Connection Queue
latest.notes: Around the world, renewable energy and storage projects are waiting years in queues before they can come onto the grid. Even as the energy transition accelerated, many of these queues continued to run on the conventional first-come, first-served basis. So speculative proposals could get ahead of projects that were practical to build, providing a headwind on how fast the transition could move. Britain is one example, where in December 2025, its National Energy System Operator (NESO) told a committee of Parliament that 70% of the projects in its queue would never be built. Nine months later, Britain’s Minister for Energy told another committee that the connection dates many projects had been holding were “a work of fiction in most cases.” What would it take to get real projects onto the grid faster, so that they can cut carbon emissions and make our energy supply more sustainable? A version of that question is under debate in the US as this episode is released. Congress is considering a wide-ranging bill on permitting and the power grid, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which, among other changes, would reform interconnection queues to discourage speculative projects. In this episode of our documentary series, we look at the reforms and proposals in Britain, the US, Europe and Australia for getting projects through these queues faster and building the power lines they need, drawing on public recordings and episodes featuring conversations with our host Chris Nelder. We’ll hear why, nearly a decade ago, a state utility commission could tell a company that wanted to build a multi-state power line that it couldn’t even apply for a permit, because it had no customers in that state. And we’ll hear about tenants in the German city of Neumünster who have spent two years looking at the solar panels on the roofs of their buildings, still waiting for the local grid operator to connect them. latest.notes: Since industry record-keeping began in 1976, global solar capacity has grown every single year. That streak, however, could end in 2026. Every year since 2017, Jenny Chase, a solar and clean power analyst at BloombergNEF, has published an annual thread on social media outlining her most significant — and sometimes controversial — takes on the state of the global solar industry. In this year’s thread , she makes the case that this will be the global industry’s first down year for new builds. In this episode, Shayle unpacks the highlights from Jenny’s solar "State of the Union." They discuss her marquee prediction, and dig deeper to make sense of what this saturation point means for the global energy transition. latest.title: Data centers need to earn their power [partner content]
latest.notes: Data center developers face a difficult choice: wait years for a traditional grid connection, or build their own power systems and operate independently of the grid. But a third path is emerging. By bringing onsite generation, batteries, and sophisticated software controls, data centers can be more flexible when the grid is constrained — and potentially connect to the system faster. But batteries alone don't make a data center flexible. They need to be coordinated in real time to meet the demands of the facility, the utility, and the broader electricity market. And the stakes go well beyond the data center industry. If these new loads can help utilities avoid expensive infrastructure upgrades, they could also help limit electricity bill increases for a wider range of consumers. In this partner episode, produced in collaboration with Verse, Stephen Lacey talks with Seyed Madaeni, co-founder and CEO of Verse. They talk about the growing role of flexibility in connecting data centers. How do we ensure the rush to power AI allows us to build a more distributed, resilient, and affordable electricity system? This episode was produced in partnership with Verse. Verse helps large energy buyers secure power faster and manage electricity costs through intelligent software that optimizes energy procurement, batteries, and onsite power assets. Learn how Verse is helping data centers unlock faster grid connections through flexibility.

latest.title: Clean firm power’s next test: Can nuclear and geothermal scale economically?
latest.notes: Rising electricity demand, especially from AI and data centers, has brought nuclear and geothermal back into focus as sources of clean, firm power. But demand, corporate partnerships and policy support are not the same as projects delivering affordable electricity on time. The central question is whether both technologies can turn renewed momentum into repeatable deployment. Host Caitlin Connolly, Senior Analyst at Wood Mackenzie, is joined by Jenifer Shafer, professor of chemistry and Ben L. Fryrear Presidential Chair at Colorado School of Mines, and Anna Littlefield, Geothermal and Low Carbon Technologies Program Manager at the Payne Institute for Public Policy. They compare what is driving this moment and where the routes to scale diverge. On nuclear, uprates and restarts could add capacity sooner than new builds, while small modular reactors are more likely to arrive in the 2030s. Shafer explains how fuel recycling could improve fuel security and reduce the amount of material requiring disposal, but would not remove the need for a repository. Cost, safeguards and social license remain central challenges, while progress through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission is a key signal to watch. Enhanced geothermal systems aim to reach heat in deep rock beyond the limited areas served by conventional hydrothermal resources. Drilling and reservoir engineering have advanced, but the test now is whether projects can sustain heat flow economically over time while managing water loss, scaling, corrosion and reservoir performance. Littlefield points to power purchase agreements scheduled for the 2028 to 2030 period as an important test of delivery, not yet proof of scale. Colorado’s permitting and development efforts, including work to assess whether treated oil and gas produced water can support geothermal circulation, may offer lessons for other states. The technologies face different constraints: nuclear must address fuel, waste and project execution, while geothermal must prove durable reservoirs and manage water and induced-seismicity concerns. Both also depend on community trust. The guests argue that developers need to listen to local concerns and share monitoring data, rather than assume technical explanations alone will win support. Over the next five years, the clearest evidence will be projects that reach operation and perform as promised, alongside nuclear licensing progress and geothermal’s ability to deliver contracted power reliably. latest.title: 255. Digital Twins for Grids - Nov26
latest.notes: Geographic Information System (GIS) are used by all Infrastructure managers to map where physical assets are. But they are mostly a glorified version of Google Maps. Here come digital twins, where new systems seemingly integrate and unifies fragmented software tools for GIS mapping, engineering design, asset records, and weather tracking. Digital Twins sit at the intersection of 3D geospatial reality modelling, structural engineering, and utility asset management. And Neara is one of the fastest growing start-ups in that segment, once dominated by the Siemens and Schneider Electric. Working with Utlities take time, as you go from Pilot to Pilot and certain are even reluctant to know what is going on in their grid, for fear of having to do something about it. And still, Neara has achieved massive progress giving visibility to its clients (SoCal, Centerpoint, Scottish Power, ESB, Ausgrid). Originally from Australia and now global, Neara has reached a valuation of almost 1bnUSD after a series of successful capital raises. Gerard and Laurent bring in Taco Engelaar, Senior Vice President & Managing Director at Neara. Named one of Time Magazine’s 100 Most Influential Companies in 2024, Taco leads Neara’s team and operations in the UK and Europe, building partnerships and developing relationships across the continent. He also oversees Neara’s international expansion in the EMEA & LATAM regions. With Taco, we discuss the benefits of digital twins, how they are integrated within clients, which are slow and conservative, and how they are saving the grids by optimising Maintenance, reducing the need for new built, and are accelerating the connection of datacenters.

latest.title: Azolla Ventures: Using Catalytic Capital to Fund Novel Climate Technologies
latest.notes: Many of the technologies needed to address climate change are not easy to fund with the traditional venture capital model that is developed around software. They can require significant upfront investment, take years to reach commercial scale, and operate in sectors where markets and regulations are still evolving.Amy Duffuor, Co-Founder and General Partner at Azolla Ventures, joins Climate Rising to explain how catalytic capital can help bridge that financing gap. She describes Azolla’s approach to investing in early-stage climate technologies that have the potential for large-scale emissions reductions but may be too early, capital-intensive, or unconventional for traditional venture investors. Amy shares how Azolla sources and evaluates investments, why the firm prioritizes additionality and freestanding unit economics when choosing what to fund, and how it supports founders beyond providing capital. She also shares examples from long-duration energy storage company Noon Energy and geothermal company Zanskar, and discusses emerging opportunities in super pollutants, water, and other underfunded areas of climate technology. Note: guest host John Mulliken is both an HBS professor and an Operating Partner at Azolla Ventures.

latest.title: What the World Fears of a Lame-Duck Trump: A Conversation With Daniel W. Drezner and Elizabeth N. Saunders
latest.notes: Donald Trump’s second-term foreign policy has brought some continuity, with the president acting on long-standing fixations on trade and allies and more. It’s also brought some surprises, especially when it comes to the use of military force. Now, Trump is entering the lame-duck period of his presidency. And with larger-than-expected midterm wins, Democrats are making grand promises about ending the war in Iran, exposing globe-spanning corruption, and much else. In a recent article for Foreign Affairs , Daniel Drezner, a professor of international politics at Tufts, and Elizabeth Saunders, a professor of political science at Columbia, considered what Trump can, and cannot, achieve internationally in the next two years. Dan Kurtz-Phelan spoke with them on Wednesday, November 18, about the possible consequences of Trump’s lame-duck foreign policy—and about the debates within both parties about what should come next. You can find sources, transcripts, and more episodes of The Foreign Affairs Interview at https://www.foreignaffairs.com/podcasts/foreign-affairs-interview.

latest.title: The new AI philanthropists and the climate finance divide at COP31
latest.notes: This week, we explore Anthropic’s colossal stock market debut in the context of global development. We unpack what this historic initial public offer means and how the wealth created by this milestone could reshape philanthropy and unlock a new wave of grants — including which global issues these AI philanthropists might target. We also discuss how artificial intelligence is being addressed at 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, or COP31 — particularly the challenge of aligning data-center expansion with climate goals and how the technology fits into the broader theme of electrification. While encouraging ideas are emerging, conversations are stalling over financing. At COP31, it is becoming apparent that multilateral development banks are increasingly divided over their climate commitments. With the World Bank Group dropping its 45% climate finance target and the Inter-American Development Bank considering a similar move, the European Investment Bank appears to be preparing to take the lead on climate financing. latest.title: From the Frontlines of the Fight Against Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
latest.notes: The Ebola outbreak in the eastern regions of the Democratic Republic of the Congo is now the second-largest outbreak on record—and is on pace to surpass the 2014 West Africa Ebola outbreak. There have been more than 11,000 confirmed cases and over 5,000 deaths. But unlike the previous outbreak, there has been no massive, coordinated international response. The outbreak is raging, and much of the world seems to be shrugging it off. I'm joined today by Shweta Shah, Prosper Global's Ebola Program Portfolio Director, who speaks with me from Bunia, the epicenter of this outbreak. She explains how the outbreak spiraled out of control so quickly, how the ongoing conflict has fueled its spread, and why community-based interventions offer the best hope of containing it.

latest.title: Who Should and Shouldn't Get Aid? With Stefan Dercon and Charles Kenny
latest.notes: CGD's Rachel Glennerster speaks with the University of Oxford's Stefan Dercon and CGD's Charles Kenny about how donors should weigh poverty, political commitment, and the potential for impact when deciding where aid goes; whether aid can support both economic transformation and essential services in the poorest countries; and what reforms to the World Bank's IDA funding and OECD aid eligibility rules could help make aid more effective.
